intro: At McGill, B. Barry Levy ran the M.A. stream in the History of the Jewish Interpretation of the Bible: each student took one verse or passage and traced its Jewish interpretation through some hundred primary sources, from the Bible itself to the medieval world and beyond (the stream's thesis course, JWST 691, is described as 'a study of the history of Jewish interpretation of one verse, based on 100 primary sources'). These are the verse theses of that stream that have been collected so far — each one is attached to its verse in the Mega Bible.

theses.author: Deborah Abecassis
theses.blurb: A judge vows to sacrifice whatever comes out of his house to greet him — and his daughter comes out dancing. Abecassis samples the Jewish responses from ancient times through the twentieth century: more than two dozen interpreters solving the text's problems, and largely declining its ethical one.
theses.title: Jephthah's Daughter in the Jewish Exegetical Tradition

theses.author: Dan Rand
theses.blurb: After the golden calf, Moses pleads “show me Your glory” and is answered with a hidden face. Rand reads the medieval Jewish interpreters of the passage against each other — where their exegesis ends and their ideology begins.
theses.title: The Interplay of Exegesis and Ideology in the Jewish Medieval Interpretations of Exodus 33:12–23

theses.author: Bryna Brodt
theses.blurb: The serpent appears in one chapter of the Bible and was debated ever after. Brodt sorts the Jewish readings — literal, allegorical and mythical — from the Bible through the thirteenth century.
theses.title: The Serpent's Identity in Genesis 3: A History of Jewish Interpretation from the Bible Through the Thirteenth Century

theses.author: Deborah Weiser
theses.blurb: Why is kindling singled out from all labour? Weiser surveys לא־תבערו אשׁ from its biblical inception through the twentieth century and the advent of electricity.
theses.title: Fire and the Sabbath: A Look at Exodus 35:3 and the Jewish Exegetical History of the Biblical Prohibition Against Using Fire on the Sabbath Day

theses.author: Tobi Liebman
theses.blurb: Is Deuteronomy 22:5 about keeping the sexes separate or about cross-dressing? Liebman follows the exegetes through כלי־גבר and שׂמלת אשׁה, clause by clause.
theses.title: The Jewish Exegetical History of Deuteronomy 22:5: Required Gender Separation or Prohibited Cross-Dressing?

theses.author: Andrea Dawn Lobel
theses.blurb: החדשׁ הזה לכם — the Bible's first calendrical commandment, and the calendars built on it: Septuagint and Pseudepigrapha, Tannaim and Amoraim, Qumran, Samaritans and Karaites.
theses.title: The Green Ears of Xanthicus: Calendrical Interpretations of Exodus 12:1–2 in Jewish and Sectarian Sources from the Biblical Through Medieval Periods

theses.author: Maayan Lustigman
theses.blurb: Judah and Tamar — the chapter that interrupts the Joseph story and seeds the Davidic line — traced as a dialogue among its interpreters, biblical to modern.
theses.title: “What a Breach You Have Made for Yourself!”: The History of Jewish Interpretations of Genesis 38

theses.author: Alyssa Ovadis
theses.blurb: The first command in Eden names a tree but never its fruit. Ovadis follows how Jewish interpretation and art alternately abstracted the fruit of עץ הדעת טוב ורע into a symbol and concretized it into a specific fruit.
theses.title: Abstraction and Concretization of the Fruit of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil As Seen Through Biblical Interpretation and Art

theses.author: Briah Cahana
theses.blurb: Shiphrah and Puah defy Pharaoh and are rewarded with “houses” — but who were they? Cahana traces the midwives' identities through a large sample of Jewish and Christian interpretation, from the fourth century BCE to the fourteenth century CE.
theses.title: The Enigmatic Meyalledot Ha'ivriyyot: A History of Interpretation of Exodus 1:15-21 from Antiquity to the Medieval Period

theses.author: Irving M. Binik
theses.blurb: Rahab of Jericho — innkeeper or harlot, convert or ancestress of prophets — from antiquity to the medieval period. Joshua 2 is read each year as the haftarah of Shelach.
theses.title: Rahab the Prostitute: A History of Interpretation from Antiquity to the Medieval Period

title: The History of a Verse
